items.stem: Which metal is extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
items.answer: zinc
items.markingKey: Metals below carbon in the reactivity series (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) are extracted by reduction with carbon.

items.stem: Explain why electrolysis is expensive compared with reduction by carbon.
items.answer: It needs large amounts of electricity to melt the ore and decompose it.

items.stem: Explain why gold and silver were among the first metals used by humans, whereas aluminium was not extracted until the 19th century.
items.answer: Gold and silver are unreactive and found native; aluminium is very reactive and its compounds can only be decomposed by electrolysis, which needed electricity.

items.stem: 40.5 g of CuO is heated with carbon. 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂. Calculate the maximum mass of copper that can be obtained.
8.00 g of SnO₂ is heated with carbon. SnO₂ + C → Sn + CO₂. Calculate the maximum mass of tin that can be obtained.
Ethan reads that copper is extracted from copper(II) oxide by heating it with carbon. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reduction. (b) Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted in the same way.
items.answer: (a) 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ (b) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; electrolysis is needed.

items.stem: Why must aluminium be extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?
options: Carbon reacts with aluminium to form a carbide only
Aluminium is less reactive than carbon
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon
items.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon
items.markingKey: Carbon cannot remove oxygen from oxides of metals above it in the series.

items.stem: Explain why carbon is used to extract zinc but not magnesium.
items.answer: Carbon is more reactive than zinc so it removes oxygen from zinc oxide; magnesium is more reactive than carbon.

items.stem: Explain why reduction is defined as the loss of oxygen in extraction reactions.
items.answer: The metal oxide gives up its oxygen to the reducing agent (carbon) to leave the metal.

items.stem: For the reaction 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, giving a reason in each case.
items.answer: CuO is reduced (loses oxygen); carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen).

items.stem: For the reaction ZnO + C → Zn + CO, identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, giving a reason in each case.
items.answer: ZnO is reduced (loses oxygen); carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen).

items.stem: In a small smelter, 2000 kg of ore containing 85% CuO by mass is heated with coke. (a) Identify the oxidising agent and explain your choice. (b) Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted in the same way.
items.answer: (a) CuO: it gives oxygen to carbon (it is reduced). (b) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; electrolysis is needed.

items.stem: Felix reads that lead is extracted from lead(II) oxide by heating it with carbon. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reduction. (b) 2000 kg of ore contains 60% PbO. Calculate the maximum mass of lead produced.
items.answer: (a) 2PbO + C → 2Pb + CO₂ (b) 1110 kg
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) mass PbO = 1200 kg [1]; n = 5.38 kmol [1]; mass lead = 1110 kg [1]; total [3]

items.stem: What are the three raw materials added at the top of the blast furnace?
items.answer: hematite, coke and limestone
items.markingKey: Iron ore (hematite), coke (carbon) and limestone; hot air is blown in near the bottom.

items.stem: Explain why the molten iron and slag form two separate layers at the bottom of the furnace.
items.answer: Slag is less dense than molten iron, so it floats on top; they do not mix and can be tapped off separately.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ is described as a neutralisation.
items.answer: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and silicon(IV) oxide is an acidic oxide; they react to form a salt.

items.stem: In the blast furnace, carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide. Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
items.answer: CO₂ + C → 2CO

items.stem: In the blast furnace, coke burns in hot air, releasing heat. Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction and state why it is important to the process.
items.answer: C + O₂ → CO₂; it raises the temperature of the furnace.

items.stem: In the blast furnace, calcium oxide reacts with silicon(IV) oxide impurities to form slag. Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction and state why it is important to the process.
items.answer: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃; it removes sandy impurities as slag.

items.stem: A diagram of a blast furnace shows raw materials entering at the top, hot air blown in near the base, and two tap holes at the bottom. (a) Name the three solid raw materials. (b) Explain, with equations, how sandy impurities are removed.
items.answer: (a) Hematite (iron ore), coke and limestone. (b) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ — slag floats on the iron and is tapped off.

items.stem: Tomás is writing a report on the blast furnace used to extract iron from hematite (75% Fe₂O₃). (a) Calculate the maximum mass of iron produced from 100 tonnes of the ore. (b) Name two gases that leave the top of the furnace. (c) Suggest one use for the slag.
items.answer: (a) 52.5 tonnes (b) Nitrogen and carbon dioxide (also some carbon monoxide). (c) Road building or making cement.

items.stem: Which substance reduces iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace?
items.answer: carbon monoxide

items.stem: What is the purpose of limestone in the blast furnace?
options: To remove acidic impurities such as silicon(IV) oxide as slag
items.answer: To remove acidic impurities such as silicon(IV) oxide as slag
items.markingKey: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag).

items.stem: Explain why the waste gases leaving the top of the blast furnace include nitrogen.
items.answer: Hot air is blown in; the nitrogen in it is unreactive and passes through unchanged.

items.stem: Explain why carbon monoxide is described as the reducing agent in the blast furnace.
items.answer: It removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of iron, in tonnes, that can be extracted from 10 tonnes of pure iron(III) oxide. (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂)
items.answer: 7.00 tonnes

items.stem: A blast furnace is charged with 400 t of hematite and 266 t of iron is tapped off. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Determine the percentage purity of the ore, assuming all the iron(III) oxide was reduced.

An ore contains 64% iron(III) oxide by mass. Calculate the maximum mass of iron, in tonnes, that can be extracted from 80 tonnes of the ore. (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂) Calculate also the volume of carbon monoxide, in m³ at r.t.p., needed to reduce the iron(III) oxide (1 m³ = 1000 dm³).

A diagram of a blast furnace shows raw materials entering at the top, hot air blown in near the base, and two tap holes at the bottom. (a) Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide. (b) Suggest one use for the slag.
items.answer: (a) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (b) Road building or making cement.

items.stem: A diagram of a blast furnace shows raw materials entering at the top, hot air blown in near the base, and two tap holes at the bottom. (a) Name the three solid raw materials. (b) Describe, with equations, how carbon monoxide is formed in the furnace. (c) Suggest one use for the slag.
items.answer: (a) Hematite (iron ore), coke and limestone. (b) Coke burns: C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ reacts with more coke: CO₂ + C → 2CO. (c) Road building or making cement.

items.stem: What is the main ore of aluminium?
items.answer: bauxite
items.markingKey: Bauxite is purified to give aluminium oxide (alumina).

items.stem: Explain why the aluminium oxide must be molten or dissolved before electrolysis.
items.answer: The ions must be free to move to the electrodes; in the solid they are held in a lattice.

items.stem: Explain why the extraction of aluminium uses large amounts of energy.
items.answer: Electricity is needed to keep the electrolyte molten and to decompose Al₂O₃ (strong bonds), and the process runs at about 950 °C.

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 306 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide. (2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂)
items.answer: 162 tonnes

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 510 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide. (2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂)
items.answer: 270 tonnes

items.stem: Lina visits an aluminium plant where 102 tonnes of aluminium oxide are electrolysed each day. (a) Explain why cryolite is used. (b) Give two reasons why recycling aluminium is better than extracting it.
items.answer: (a) Aluminium oxide dissolves in molten cryolite at a much lower temperature than its melting point, saving energy; it also improves conductivity. (b) Saves energy; conserves bauxite; less mining damage; less CO₂ from anodes and power generation.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium smelters are often built near hydroelectric power stations.
items.answer: They need huge amounts of electricity; hydroelectric power is cheap and renewable.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction at the anode is oxidation.
items.answer: Oxide ions lose electrons to form oxygen molecules: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻.

items.stem: Explain why recycling aluminium cans saves more energy than extracting new aluminium.
items.answer: Melting scrap aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy needed for electrolysis of bauxite; it also saves ore.

items.stem: Bauxite mined near Dhaka contains 63% aluminium oxide by mass. Calculate the mass of aluminium that could be made from 500 tonnes of this bauxite. 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂
Bauxite mined near Cairo contains 56% aluminium oxide by mass. Calculate the mass of aluminium that could be made from 75 tonnes of this bauxite. 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂

An aluminium smelter in Hanoi electrolyses purified bauxite dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 °C. (a) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (b) Write the half-equation at the anode. (c) Give two reasons why recycling aluminium is better than extracting it.
items.answer: (a) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (b) 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (c) Saves energy; conserves bauxite; less mining damage; less CO₂ from anodes and power generation.

items.stem: An aluminium smelter in Dhaka electrolyses purified bauxite dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 °C. (a) Write the half-equation at the anode. (b) Explain why the anodes must be replaced regularly, with an equation. (c) Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 510 tonnes of aluminium oxide. (d) Explain why the molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.
items.answer: (a) 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (b) Oxygen reacts with the hot carbon: C + O₂ → CO₂, so the anodes burn away. (c) 270 tonnes (d) It is denser than the electrolyte, so it sinks and is siphoned off.

items.stem: Which two substances are needed for iron to rust?
items.answer: oxygen and water
items.markingKey: Iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide.

items.stem: Explain why a galvanised bucket does not rust even when the zinc coating is scratched.
items.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes (loses electrons) in preference to the iron — sacrificial protection.

items.stem: Explain why a tin-plated food can rusts quickly once the tin layer is scratched.
items.answer: Tin is less reactive than iron; once exposed, the iron corrodes in preference to the tin (faster than unprotected iron).

items.stem: An engineer proposes attaching blocks of tin to a steel water tank to stop it rusting. Deduce whether this would work and explain your answer in terms of electron loss.
items.answer: No: tin is less reactive than iron, so the iron would still lose electrons; it may even rust faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark reactivity comparison; 1 mark electron loss explanation [3]

items.stem: An engineer proposes attaching blocks of aluminium to a steel pipeline buried in damp soil to stop it rusting. Deduce whether this would work and explain your answer in terms of electron loss.
items.answer: Yes: aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons and corrodes instead of the iron (sacrificial protection).
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark reactivity comparison; 1 mark electron loss explanation [3]

items.stem: Elena sets up four test-tubes to investigate rusting and leaves them for one week. tube 1: an iron nail coated in grease, in tap water; tube 2: an iron nail in pure nitrogen gas with water; tube 3: an iron nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride; tube 4: an iron nail wrapped in a strip of copper, in tap water. (a) Explain why galvanised steel is used for roofing sheets. (b) Describe how boiling the water and adding oil changes the conditions.
items.answer: (a) Zinc coating is a barrier and, if scratched, zinc corrodes in preference to iron (sacrificial). (b) Boiling removes dissolved oxygen; the oil layer stops oxygen from the air redissolving.

items.stem: What is the chemical name for rust?
items.answer: hydrated iron(III) oxide
items.markingKey: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

items.stem: Explain how barrier methods prevent rusting.
items.answer: They stop oxygen and water from reaching the surface of the iron.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of electrons, how sacrificial protection works.
items.answer: The more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium) loses electrons more readily than iron, so it is oxidised instead and the iron does not form ions.

items.stem: An engineer proposes attaching blocks of silver to a steel pipeline buried in damp soil to stop it rusting. Deduce whether this would work and explain your answer in terms of electron loss.
items.answer: No: silver is less reactive than iron, so the iron would still lose electrons; it may even rust faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark reactivity comparison; 1 mark electron loss explanation [3]

items.stem: An iron nail of mass 11.2 g rusts completely to form iron(III) oxide (ignore the water of hydration). 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Calculate the mass of iron(III) oxide formed and the volume of oxygen used at r.t.p., in dm³.

An iron nail of mass 2.80 g rusts completely to form iron(III) oxide (ignore the water of hydration). 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Calculate the mass of iron(III) oxide formed and the volume of oxygen used at r.t.p., in dm³.
Why is gold found as the uncombined element in the Earth’s crust?
items.answer: It is very unreactive
items.markingKey: Gold does not react with oxygen or water, so it occurs native.

items.stem: Explain why recycling metals such as aluminium is important.
items.answer: It saves ores (finite resources) and energy, reduces mining damage and landfill.

items.stem: 22.3 g of SnO₂ is heated with carbon. SnO₂ + C → Sn + CO₂. Calculate the maximum mass of tin that can be obtained.

In a small smelter, 500 kg of ore containing 85% SnO₂ by mass is heated with coke. (a) Identify the oxidising agent and explain your choice. (b) Suggest one environmental problem caused by extracting metals from ores.
items.answer: (a) SnO₂: it gives oxygen to carbon (it is reduced). (b) Mining scars the landscape/habitat loss; CO₂ from burning coke contributes to climate change; waste rock.

items.stem: A mining company in Toronto extracts copper from an ore containing CuO. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reduction. (b) Suggest one environmental problem caused by extracting metals from ores. (c) Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted in the same way.
items.answer: (a) 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ (b) Mining scars the landscape/habitat loss; CO₂ from burning coke contributes to climate change; waste rock. (c) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; electrolysis is needed.

items.stem: What is the chemical name of slag?
items.answer: calcium silicate

items.stem: Explain why the iron from the blast furnace is usually converted into steel.
items.answer: Blast-furnace iron contains about 4% carbon, making it brittle; removing most of the carbon and adding other elements gives stronger, less brittle steel.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why carbon monoxide is described as the reducing agent in the blast furnace. (b) Explain why the iron from the blast furnace is usually converted into steel.
items.answer: (a) It removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide. (b) Blast-furnace iron contains about 4% carbon, making it brittle; removing most of the carbon and adding other elements gives stronger, less brittle steel.

items.stem: In the blast furnace, limestone undergoes thermal decomposition. Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
items.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of iron, in tonnes, that can be extracted from 200 tonnes of pure iron(III) oxide. (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂)
items.answer: 140 tonnes

items.stem: A steelworks in Manila feeds 400 tonnes of hematite ore containing 70% iron(III) oxide into its blast furnace each day. (a) Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of iron produced from 400 tonnes of the ore.
items.answer: (a) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (b) 196 tonnes

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the half-equation at the cathode? (b) Why do the carbon anodes need to be replaced regularly?
items.answer: (a) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (b) They react with the oxygen produced to form carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: (a) Aluminium ions gain electrons (reduction). (b) C + O₂ → CO₂ at high temperature burns the anodes away.

items.stem: Grace writes that in the extraction of aluminium "cryolite is the ore of aluminium". Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: Bauxite is the ore; cryolite is a solvent that lowers the melting point of the electrolyte.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifying the error; 1 mark correct chemistry [2]

items.stem: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode in the extraction of aluminium, and state whether it is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; oxidation (loss of electrons)
items.markingKey: 1 mark equation; 1 mark oxidation/reduction with reason [2]

items.stem: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode in the extraction of aluminium, and state whether it is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; reduction (gain of electrons)
items.markingKey: 1 mark equation; 1 mark oxidation/reduction with reason [2]

items.stem: Lina visits an aluminium plant where 102 tonnes of aluminium oxide are electrolysed each day. (a) Explain why cryolite is used. (b) Explain why the anodes must be replaced regularly, with an equation. (c) Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 102 tonnes of aluminium oxide.
items.answer: (a) Aluminium oxide dissolves in molten cryolite at a much lower temperature than its melting point, saving energy; it also improves conductivity. (b) Oxygen reacts with the hot carbon: C + O₂ → CO₂, so the anodes burn away. (c) 54.0 tonnes

items.stem: Explain why cars rust faster in coastal cities and where salt is spread on winter roads.
items.answer: Dissolved salt (ions) increases the rate of rusting.

items.stem: A student sets up an iron nail in boiled water covered with a layer of oil. Predict whether the nail rusts after a week, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: Does not rust: boiling removes dissolved oxygen and the oil stops air dissolving.

items.stem: A tin-plated steel roofing sheet in Jakarta is scratched, exposing the iron underneath. Predict whether the iron at the scratch will rust. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Yes: tin is less reactive than iron, so the iron loses electrons and rusts, even faster than unprotected iron.

items.stem: Priya sets up four test-tubes to investigate rusting and leaves them for one week. tube 1: an iron nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride; tube 2: an iron nail in tap water, open to the air; tube 3: an iron nail in salt water, open to the air; tube 4: an iron nail in boiled water covered with a layer of oil. (a) Predict in which tubes the nail rusts. (b) State the conditions needed for rusting. (c) Write the word equation for rusting.
items.answer: (a) 2, 3 (b) Water and oxygen both present. (c) iron + water + oxygen → hydrated iron(III) oxide

items.stem: In the reaction 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, what happens to the copper(II) oxide?
options: It is decomposed by heat alone
items.answer: It is reduced
items.markingKey: CuO loses oxygen: reduction. Carbon gains oxygen: oxidation.

items.stem: Zinc is obtained by reduction of the oxide with carbon, while magnesium is obtained by electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride. Use the reactivity series to explain the difference.
items.answer: Zinc is below carbon and magnesium is above carbon in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon need electrolysis; metals below carbon can be reduced by carbon; very unreactive metals are found native.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each metal positioned relative to carbon; 1 mark rule linking position to method [3]

options: It provides heat and produces carbon dioxide

items.answer: (a) Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and silicon(IV) oxide is an acidic oxide; they react to form a salt. (b) It removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

items.answer: 112 tonnes

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 1020 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide. (2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂)
items.answer: 540 tonnes

items.answer: Does not rust: no oxygen is present.

items.answer: Yes: paint is only a barrier; once broken, water and oxygen reach the iron.
